title: Aortic valve replacement (surgical)
subtitle: Outline level: sternotomy, bypass, cardioplegia, excision, sizing, implantation, de-airing and weaning

sources.title: 2021 ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease
2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease

indications: Severe symptomatic aortic stenosis or regurgitation where the heart team recommends surgery (age, risk, anatomy and patient choice weighed against transcatheter replacement).
Severe aortic valve disease at the time of other cardiac surgery; infective endocarditis meeting surgical criteria.
contraindications: Prohibitive surgical risk where transcatheter or medical therapy is chosen by the heart team.
Active infection elsewhere that would seed the prosthesis (except endocarditis surgery).
preparation: Heart team decision; echocardiography, coronary angiography, dental review.
Choose the prosthesis with the patient: mechanical (lifelong anticoagulation) or biological (durability).
Consent: death, stroke, bleeding and re-operation, heart block needing a pacemaker, infection, paravalvular leak, and prosthesis-related long-term risks.
positioning: Supine, arms tucked, a roll between the shoulder blades, chest, abdomen and legs prepared for conduit or femoral access.
equipment: Cardiac surgery set, sternal saw, cardiopulmonary bypass circuit, cannulae, cross-clamp, cardioplegia delivery, valve sizers and the chosen prosthesis, pledgeted sutures, transoesophageal echocardiography.
anatomy: The aortic root: the three leaflets and sinuses, the coronary ostia (left and right), the annulus with the conduction tissue (bundle of His) below the commissure between the right and non-coronary cusps, the anterior mitral leaflet beneath.
criticalSafety: Full heparinisation with a confirmed ACT before cannulation.
Remove all calcium debris and keep it out of the ventricle and coronaries.
Check the coronary ostia are clear after seating the valve; de-air before the clamp comes off.
structuresAtRisk: Aortic wall (dissection at cannulation or clamp)
commonErrors: Calcium embolising into the ventricle or coronaries.
Deep sutures near the conduction tissue.
complications: Paravalvular leak, prosthetic endocarditis, valve thrombosis.
postop: Intensive care; drains monitored for bleeding and tamponade.
Pacing wires kept until rhythm is stable; anticoagulation per prosthesis.
Echocardiogram before discharge; endocarditis prevention and dental care advice.

steps.emphasis: Record the prosthesis choice and the reasons.
Confirm the prosthesis type and size range available, blood products, perfusion and echo ready.
Supine, arms tucked, roll between the shoulder blades.
Protamine after decannulation, watching for reaction.
Count every swab, needle and pledget before closing the pericardium and sternum.
Hand over the prosthesis, bypass and cross-clamp times, rhythm, pacing settings and the anticoagulation plan.

step.avr.cpb.title: Heparinisation, cannulation and starting bypass
step.avr.cpb.why: Bypass lets the heart be stopped and opened. Cannulating an unheparinised patient, or a diseased aorta, risks clotting the circuit or dissecting the aorta.
how: Give heparin and confirm an adequate activated clotting time before cannulation.
Place purse strings and cannulate the ascending aorta (checked by epiaortic scan if calcified) and the right atrium.
Start bypass with the perfusionist, confirming flows and pressures.
pitfalls: Cannulating before the ACT is confirmed.
Cannulating a calcified aorta without assessment.

step.avr.cardioplegia.title: Cross-clamp and cardioplegia
step.avr.cardioplegia.why: Cardioplegia arrests and protects the heart. In aortic regurgitation antegrade root cardioplegia leaks into the ventricle, so it is given directly into the coronary ostia or retrogradely.
how: Apply the cross-clamp to the ascending aorta.
Give cardioplegia antegrade (root), via the coronary ostia, or retrograde via the coronary sinus as appropriate; repeat at intervals.
Vent the left ventricle to keep it decompressed.

step.avr.excise.title: Aortotomy, leaflet excision and decalcification
step.avr.excise.why: Calcium must be removed to seat the prosthesis, but fragments that fall into the ventricle or coronaries cause stroke or infarction.
how: Make an oblique or transverse aortotomy above the sinotubular junction.
Excise the leaflets and debride calcium from the annulus, with a sponge in the ventricle to catch debris.
Irrigate and suction thoroughly; avoid creating a hole in the annulus or the anterior mitral leaflet.

step.avr.sutures.title: Sizing and placing the annular sutures
step.avr.sutures.why: Correct sizing avoids patient-prosthesis mismatch; suture depth near the conduction tissue decides whether the patient needs a pacemaker.
how: Size the annulus with the manufacturer's sizers.
Place pledgeted horizontal mattress sutures around the annulus, keeping them superficial below the right-non-coronary commissure.
Pass them through the prosthesis sewing ring in order.
pitfalls: Deep bites at the commissure over the conduction tissue.

step.avr.seat.title: Seating the valve and checking the coronaries
step.avr.seat.why: A properly seated valve does not leak around its edge or block a coronary ostium; mechanical leaflets must move freely.
how: Lower the prosthesis into the annulus and tie the sutures evenly.
Check the coronary ostia are not obstructed by the sewing ring or struts.
For a mechanical valve, test leaflet movement; for a biological valve, check the struts clear the ostia.

step.avr.deair.title: Closing the aorta and de-airing
step.avr.deair.why: Air left in the left heart embolises to the brain or the right coronary artery when the heart starts to eject.
how: Close the aortotomy in two layers.
De-air the left heart through the root vent and the ventricular vent while the anaesthetist inflates the lungs; check with transoesophageal echo.
Remove the cross-clamp with the root vent running.
structuresAtRisk: Brain and right coronary artery (air embolism)

step.avr.wean.title: Weaning from bypass and checking the valve
step.avr.wean.why: Transoesophageal echo confirms the valve works before decannulation, when it can still be fixed.
how: Rewarm, establish rhythm (pacing if heart block), and wean from bypass with the anaesthetist and perfusionist.
Echo: gradient across the valve, any paravalvular leak, ventricular function, aortic root.
A significant leak or failure to wean means going back on bypass; discuss as a team.
